XPoSat: Studying X-rays from Astronomical Sources

XPoSat stands for X-ray Polarimeter Satellite. ISRO launched it on 1 January 2024.

XPoSat is India's first dedicated mission for measuring the polarisation of X-rays emitted by astronomical sources. Its observations help scientists investigate energetic environments associated with objects such as neutron stars and black holes.

What Is X-ray Polarisation?

X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation, like visible light, but with much higher photon energies. Certain astronomical objects produce X-rays through energetic physical processes.

Polarisation describes the orientation of the electric field oscillations in electromagnetic radiation. Measuring the degree and direction of X-ray polarisation gives scientists additional information about the conditions in which the radiation was produced.

For example, X-rays from matter in the extreme environment around a black hole or neutron star can carry information about that environment. Their polarisation provides a different type of evidence from ordinary measurements of brightness alone.

Scientific Objective and Instruments

XPoSat was designed primarily to investigate the polarisation of X-ray emissions from selected cosmic sources. It carries two scientific instruments:

  • POLIX: Measures the polarisation of X-rays.
  • XSPECT: Studies the energy distribution and variation with time of X-rays from astronomical sources.

These measurements complement each other. Polarisation provides information about the characteristics of the radiation, while spectral and timing measurements help scientists understand its energy and changes over time.

XPoSat is an astronomy mission operating in Earth orbit. It is not a mission to the Moon, Mars or the Sun. ISRO continued to operate the mission and make scientific data available during 2026.

XPoSat studies X-ray polarisation from astronomical sources. Aditya-L1 studies the Sun, even though some of Aditya-L1's scientific instruments also observe solar X-rays. The overall mission objectives are different.

SPADEX: Demonstrating Spacecraft Docking

SPADEX, also written SpaDeX, stands for Space Docking Experiment. It is a technology demonstration mission developed by ISRO.

The mission was launched on 30 December 2024 using the PSLV-C60 launch vehicle. It involved two small spacecraft placed into low Earth orbit.

The principal objective was to demonstrate the ability of two independent spacecraft to approach each other in orbit, connect safely and subsequently separate.

Meaning of Rendezvous, Docking and Undocking

  • Rendezvous: Two spacecraft approach one another in orbit while carefully controlling their relative positions and speeds.
  • Docking: The spacecraft make controlled contact and mechanically connect to form a joined system.
  • Undocking: The connected spacecraft separate in a controlled manner and resume independent movement.

Docking requires controlled relative motion. It is not simply a collision between two satellites. The spacecraft must approach and connect in a way that avoids damaging them.

SPADEX Spacecraft and Achievements

The two spacecraft were identified as SDX01, the nominal Chaser, and SDX02, the nominal Target. Their task was to demonstrate docking operations in Earth orbit.

ISRO achieved the first successful docking on 16 January 2025. The mission subsequently demonstrated undocking and another docking operation. Electrical power transfer between the docked spacecraft was also successfully demonstrated in April 2025.

The importance of docking technology extends beyond a single experiment. Future space activities may require separately launched spacecraft or modules to connect in orbit. Such capabilities can support space stations and more complex space exploration missions.

SPADEX Status at the Content Cutoff

According to ISRO's update dated 23 October 2026, both SPADEX spacecraft completed their core mission objectives. After their operational phase, their orbits gradually decayed, and both spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on 12 October 2026.

Thus, the mission's docking demonstration was successful, but the two experimental spacecraft were no longer in orbit at the 4 November 2026 cutoff.

SPADEX was launched in 2024, first achieved docking in 2025, and its two spacecraft re-entered the atmosphere in 2026. These dates refer to different events.

Why XPoSat and SPADEX Must Not Be Confused

The two missions illustrate different purposes of space technology. XPoSat is a scientific observatory that collects information about distant astronomical sources. SPADEX was a technology demonstration mission that tested whether two spacecraft could dock and undock in orbit.

Both were launched in 2024, but they had different objectives and produced different types of achievements.

Prelims focus

  • XPoSat: Launched on 1 January 2024; studies X-ray polarisation from astronomical sources.
  • POLIX: Measures X-ray polarisation; XSPECT: studies X-ray spectra and timing.
  • SPADEX: Launched on 30 December 2024; demonstrated spacecraft docking and undocking.
  • SPADEX first successfully docked its two satellites on 16 January 2025.
  • Both SPADEX spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on 12 October 2026.
  • Trap: XPoSat is an astronomy mission; SPADEX is a docking-technology mission, not an astronomical observatory.

[ISRO, 'PSLV-C58 / XPoSat Mission', 1 January 2024, mission objectives; ISRO, 'X-ray Polarimeter Satellite (XPoSat)', science objectives; ISRO, 'XPoSat Mission: Announcement of Opportunity for the Second AO Cycle', 22 June 2026; ISRO, 'SpaDeX Mission', 21 December 2024, objectives and mission concept; ISRO, 'ISRO Successfully Completed Docking of Two SPADEX Satellites', 16 January 2025; ISRO, 'SPADEX Mission: Successful Demonstration of Second Docking and Power Transfer', 21 April 2025; ISRO, 'SPADEX Satellites Re-entry into Earth's Atmosphere on October 12, 2026', 23 October 2026. Online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: XPoSat and SPADEX: Space Astronomy and Spacecraft Docking

body:
What Is NISAR?

NISAR stands for NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. It is an Earth observation satellite jointly developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) of the United States and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

NISAR was launched on 30 July 2025 aboard India's GSLV-F16 launch vehicle from Sriharikota.

Its main purpose is to observe Earth repeatedly and measure changes in the planet's surface and natural environment. Unlike Chandrayaan or Mangalyaan, NISAR is not designed to explore another celestial body. It studies Earth itself.

What Does NISAR Observe?

NISAR collects radar observations that help scientists study changes affecting land, water, ice and vegetation.

  • Land movement: Detecting changes in the position or shape of the ground, including deformation associated with earthquakes and other geological processes.
  • Glaciers and ice: Monitoring movement and changes in glaciers, ice sheets and related frozen regions.
  • Vegetation: Studying changes in forests, crops and other vegetation cover.
  • Soil moisture: Helping estimate the amount of water present in soil, which is useful for understanding agricultural conditions.
  • Water and natural hazards: Supporting observations related to surface water, flooding and environmental changes.

Repeated observations allow scientists to compare conditions at different times. For example, a series of radar measurements can help identify whether the ground has moved or whether agricultural soil has become wetter or drier.

How Radar-Based Earth Observation Works

Radar uses radio waves to detect objects or study their characteristics. In Earth observation, a radar instrument transmits electromagnetic signals toward the surface and measures the signals returned to it.

NISAR uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR). This technique combines radar measurements collected as a satellite moves along its orbit to produce detailed information about the surface.

Because radar supplies its own signals rather than depending on reflected sunlight, it can observe Earth's surface during day or night. Its microwave signals can also pass through many types of cloud cover, making radar especially useful when ordinary optical satellite images are obstructed by clouds.

This does not mean that radar directly reveals every feature beneath every material. The information obtained depends on the properties of the radar signals and the surface being observed.

NASA and ISRO Contributions

NISAR combines two radar systems operating at different microwave bands:

  • L-band radar: Developed by NASA.
  • S-band radar: Developed by ISRO.

Different radar wavelengths interact differently with vegetation, soil and other surface materials. Using both bands provides complementary observations that help scientists investigate environmental changes.

The basic distinction is that NISAR uses radar to observe Earth, whereas XPoSat measures X-rays originating from astronomical sources. They are not the same type of observation, even though both involve electromagnetic radiation.

Gujarat Connection: Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad

Gujarat has a direct institutional connection with NISAR through ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad.

SAC developed the Indian S-band synthetic aperture radar payload for NISAR. The payload was sent to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory for integration with NASA's L-band radar system.

Gujarat also contributed to ground-based activities supporting NISAR observations. ISRO reported that radar reference targets were deployed around Ahmedabad and other locations to support calibration of the satellite's radar measurements.

In February 2026, ISRO reported the demonstration of soil-moisture products developed using NISAR observations, including results over Ahmedabad and western Gujarat. Such measurements can support agricultural and water-resource analysis by helping scientists study soil wetness across large areas.

Gujarat connection: ISRO's Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad developed the S-band radar for NISAR. Gujarat was also used for radar calibration activities and soil-moisture observations.

Launch, Science Phase and Operational Status

NISAR was successfully launched on 30 July 2025. After launch, the spacecraft underwent activities needed to prepare its instruments for scientific observations.

ISRO announced the commencement of NISAR's science phase in November 2025. During 2026, NISAR continued collecting observations, and NASA and ISRO made scientific data products available to users.

At the 4 November 2026 content cutoff, NISAR was an active Earth observation mission in its science phase.

Placing NISAR Among India's Other Space Missions

NISAR's main objective is environmental observation, which makes it different from the other missions in this lesson. Chandrayaan investigates the Moon; Mangalyaan studied Mars; Aditya-L1 observes the Sun; XPoSat observes distant astronomical X-ray sources; and SPADEX demonstrated spacecraft docking.

The important relationship is between a mission's target and its purpose. A spacecraft observing Earth, a spacecraft studying another planet and a pair of spacecraft demonstrating docking all use space technology, but they are designed to answer different questions or prove different capabilities.

Prelims focus

  • NISAR: NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar.
  • Launch: 30 July 2025, aboard GSLV-F16.
  • Objective: Observe changes in Earth's land, ice, water and vegetation using radar.
  • Partnership: NASA developed the L-band radar; ISRO developed the S-band radar.
  • Gujarat connection: Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad, developed NISAR's S-band radar.
  • Trap: NISAR is an Earth observation satellite, not a mission to Mars or the Sun. Its radar observations are different from XPoSat's astronomical X-ray measurements.

Online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]
